note: Concept index. These are the atlas’s analytical terms, not native categories. Each one is defined here so that its use in the plates is consistent.

concepts.name: Threshold
concepts.gloss: The border between the living and the dead, maintained by prohibitions rather than by a wall.
concepts.description: Used for the set of small adjustments made around a death: the opened window, the covered mirror, the water thrown out, the body carried out. The term is analytical; the sources describe the practices, not the concept.

concepts.name: Soul
concepts.gloss: The part of the person that survives death; described in both theological and folk registers.
concepts.description: Orthodox doctrine and folk belief use the same word (*dusha*) for different constructions: a created immortal substance judged by God, and a breath-like presence that lingers near the body and must be fed and escorted. The atlas keeps the registers apart.

concepts.name: Return
concepts.gloss: The dead coming back, or being treated as if they might.
concepts.description: The returning dead are a way of talking about unfinished obligation. The atlas distinguishes the ethnographic reports (documented) from the category built on them (interpretation).

concepts.name: Purification
concepts.gloss: The washing of the body and the separation of the living from the dead.
concepts.description: Washing is both practical and symbolic. The atlas treats it as a technique for handling the dead at arm’s length, and avoids claims about its pre-Christian origin.

concepts.name: Mourning
concepts.gloss: The social and emotional work of loss, performed in public or withheld.
concepts.description: In the Russian twentieth century mourning was repeatedly reorganised: by the Church, by the Soviet state and by the family. The atlas follows the distinction between public commemoration and private grief.

concepts.name: Remembrance
concepts.gloss: The scheduled repetition of prayer, food and naming.
concepts.description: Remembrance in this atlas is a calendar and a set of objects: days three, nine and forty, the annual commemoration, the meal, the name spoken aloud. It is the most documented form of relation with the dead.

concepts.name: Memory
concepts.gloss: The use of the dead by the living — personal, familial, national.
concepts.description: Memory is treated here as a practice with owners and budgets. The state’s memory is built at memorial complexes; the family’s memory at the table and at the grave.

concepts.name: Abandonment
concepts.gloss: The state of a grave, a cemetery or a name that no one maintains.
concepts.description: Abandonment is what memory turns into when nobody tends it. The atlas documents it as a condition of the material record, and marks its own inability to survey it.

concepts.name: Afterlife
concepts.gloss: The imagined geography of the dead.
concepts.description: The atlas distinguishes the doctrinal claim (judgement, resurrection, communion with God) from the iconographic and folk geography (scales, rivers of fire, roads, places of waiting).

concepts.name: Debt
concepts.gloss: What the living owe the dead, and what an unpaid obligation is believed to produce.
concepts.description: Used for the reading, offered on plate E and on the table of plate D, that burial, washing, feeding and commemoration are obligations that can be discharged or left unpaid. The term is analytical; plate E marks the "unpaid debt" reading as the atlas’s own interpretation, not a folk category.

concepts.name: Calendar of the dead
concepts.gloss: The fixed days on which the dead are commemorated, and the ways the church and the village count them differently.
concepts.description: Covers the third, ninth and fortieth days, the parental Saturdays, Radonitsa, Semik and the Saturdays before Pokrov and St Demetrius. Plates C and U separate the church rule from local custom; the term only groups them.

concepts.name: Unclean death
concepts.gloss: A death outside the expected order, and the burial and fear attached to it.
concepts.description: Zelenin’s category of the "pledged" dead and the later dispute over it (plates E and T). It is a scholarly construction on real reports, not a taxonomy the sources show villagers sharing.

concepts.name: Reuse
concepts.gloss: The afterlife of stone, timber and ground once the dead are no longer tended.
concepts.description: Gravestones as curbs and foundations, churches as crematoria, houses left standing. Plates K, W and M record cases; reuse here names a pattern across them, not a single policy.

concepts.name: Household guardian
concepts.gloss: A being tied to a house and its occupants, whose relation to the dead is disputed.
concepts.description: The domovoy of plate S. Whether it is read as an ancestor is a question the sources answer differently; the atlas keeps the limit of that reading visible.

concepts.name: Substitution
concepts.gloss: One body, name or place standing in for many that cannot be handled individually.
concepts.description: The unknown soldier, the mass grave, the memorial that carries a figure instead of a register (plates I and L). The term names the exchange of information for ritual focus.

concepts.name: Underground
concepts.gloss: Burial and passage below the surface, in caves, cellars, tunnels and flooded ground.
concepts.description: Plates R and Q: the Pechory caves, a legend of a tunnel, drowned settlements. Descriptions of what lies below are marked by whether anything was surveyed or only reported.

concepts.name: Sacral Feeding
concepts.gloss: The ritual feeding of the dead with hot steam, memory-meal courses, kolivo, and commemorative drinks.
concepts.description: Used for practices based on the belief that the dead consume nourishment through steam, smell, or symbolic portions set aside on window sills, icon shelves, and grave mounds. Contrasts with Christian almsgiving, though frequently syncretized with it.

concepts.name: Apotropaic Taboo
concepts.gloss: Ritual prohibitions protecting the household and the living from the contagious or destructive gaze of the dead.
concepts.description: Encompasses the covering of reflective surfaces (mirrors, polished glass), prohibitions against sweeping or throwing out garbage while the dead remains in the house, carrying the corpse feet-first, and avoiding looking back when departing the cemetery.

concepts.name: Liminality
concepts.gloss: The transitional state between life and completed death, marked by spatial, temporal, and social borders.
concepts.description: Covers the critical transitional intervals (the forty days, the journey to the cemetery), spatial thresholds (doors, windows, river ferries, crossroads), and intermediate conditions where the soul has departed the flesh but not yet settled in the otherworld.
